name: Andromeda
mythology: Andromeda was the daughter of King Cepheus and Queen Cassiopeia of Aethiopia. After her mother boasted that she was more beautiful than the sea nymphs, Poseidon sent a sea monster to ravage the coast, and Andromeda was chained to a rock as a sacrifice. The hero Perseus rescued her and made her his wife.
funFact: Home to the Andromeda Galaxy (M31), the nearest large galaxy to the Milky Way and the most distant object visible to the naked eye.

name: Antlia
mythology: Antlia is a modern constellation created by French astronomer Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille in the 1750s to honor the air pump invented by physicist Denis Papin. It has no ancient mythology, reflecting the Enlightenment fashion of naming southern constellations after scientific instruments.
funFact: One of the faintest constellations in the sky; its brightest star is only magnitude 4.2.

name: Apus
mythology: Apus was introduced by Dutch navigators Keyser and de Houtman in the late 16th century, depicting the exotic bird-of-paradise of New Guinea. The name comes from Greek 'apous', meaning 'footless', since early trade specimens of the bird had their feet removed.
funFact: Apus lies very close to the south celestial pole and is never visible from mid-northern latitudes.

name: Aquarius
mythology: Aquarius represents Ganymede, a beautiful Trojan youth carried to Olympus by Zeus in the form of an eagle to serve as cup-bearer to the gods. The constellation pours water toward the mouth of the southern fish, Piscis Austrinus.
funFact: A zodiac constellation and part of the 'Sea', an ancient region of watery constellations that includes Pisces, Cetus, and Capricornus.

name: Aquila
mythology: Aquila is the eagle of Zeus, the bird that carried his thunderbolts and abducted the youth Ganymede to Olympus. In Chinese folklore, its bright star Altair is the cowherd separated from the weaver girl (Vega) by the river of the Milky Way, allowed to meet only once a year.
funFact: Altair, one corner of the Summer Triangle, is one of the closest bright stars at just 17 light-years away and spins so fast it is visibly flattened.

name: Ara
mythology: Ara is the altar on which the Olympian gods swore their oath of allegiance before their war against the Titans. In gratitude for victory, Zeus placed the altar in the sky, with the Milky Way often depicted as the smoke rising from it.
funFact: One of the 48 original constellations catalogued by Ptolemy in the 2nd century, despite being far south in the sky.

name: Aries
mythology: Aries is the ram with the golden fleece that rescued Phrixus and Helle from sacrifice, flying them across the sea. Helle fell off at the strait now called the Hellespont, but Phrixus survived and sacrificed the ram, hanging its fleece in a sacred grove where it was later sought by Jason and the Argonauts.
funFact: Around 2,000 years ago the Sun crossed into Aries at the spring equinox, which is why the equinox point is still called the 'First Point of Aries'.

name: Auriga
mythology: Auriga is usually identified as Erichthonius, a legendary king of Athens who invented the four-horse chariot to compensate for his lameness. The charioteer is traditionally drawn carrying a she-goat (the star Capella) and her kids on his arm.
funFact: Capella, the sixth-brightest star in the sky, is actually a system of four stars: two giant suns orbited by two red dwarfs.

name: Boötes
mythology: Boötes is the herdsman who drives the bears (Ursa Major and Ursa Minor) around the celestial pole with his hunting dogs, Canes Venatici. He is sometimes identified with Arcas, son of Zeus and Callisto, or with the inventor of the plough.
funFact: Arcturus is the brightest star in the northern celestial hemisphere; follow the arc of the Big Dipper's handle to find it — 'arc to Arcturus'.

name: Caelum
mythology: Caelum is another of Lacaille's 18th-century southern constellations, representing an engraver's chisel. Like his other inventions it honors the tools of arts and sciences rather than any myth.
funFact: Caelum is the eighth-smallest constellation and one of the dimmest, with no star brighter than magnitude 4.4.

name: Camelopardalis
mythology: Camelopardalis was created by Dutch astronomer Petrus Plancius in 1613 to fill the large dim region between the two bears and Perseus. Its name is the Greek word for giraffe, literally 'camel-leopard' — an animal with a camel's neck and a leopard's spots.
funFact: Despite being the 18th-largest constellation, it is so faint that on a hazy night it appears completely empty.

name: Cancer
mythology: Cancer is the crab sent by Hera to distract Heracles during his battle with the Hydra. The hero crushed it underfoot, but Hera rewarded the crab's loyalty with a place in the sky — albeit a dim one, since it failed its task.
funFact: The faintest zodiac constellation, but home to the Beehive Cluster (M44), a swarm of stars visible to the naked eye under dark skies.

name: Canes Venatici
mythology: Canes Venatici represents Asterion and Chara, the two hunting dogs held on a leash by Boötes as he pursues the Great Bear around the pole. It was formed by Johannes Hevelius in 1687 from stars that Ptolemy had left unassigned.
funFact: Its brightest star, Cor Caroli ('Heart of Charles'), was named in honor of King Charles I of England.

name: Canis Major
mythology: Canis Major is the larger of Orion's two hunting dogs, following at the hunter's heel across the winter sky. It is sometimes identified with Laelaps, a hound so swift it always caught its prey, placed in the sky by Zeus.
funFact: Contains Sirius, the brightest star in the entire night sky — the 'Dog Star', whose dawn rising marked the flooding of the Nile and the 'dog days' of summer.

name: Canis Minor
mythology: Canis Minor is Orion's smaller hunting dog. Its brightest star, Procyon, means 'before the dog' in Greek, because it rises just before Sirius. The constellation is also linked to Maera, the faithful dog of Icarius, who led his daughter to her murdered father's grave.
funFact: Procyon is one of our nearest stellar neighbors at 11.5 light-years and forms the Winter Triangle with Sirius and Betelgeuse.

name: Capricornus
mythology: Capricornus is the sea goat, often identified with the god Pan, who leapt into the Nile to escape the monster Typhon: the submerged half of his body became a fish tail while the upper half remained a goat. It is one of the oldest constellations, recognized by the Babylonians.
funFact: The Tropic of Capricorn is named for this constellation, where the Sun stood at the winter solstice in ancient times.

name: Carina
mythology: Carina is the keel of the Argo, the great ship that carried Jason and the Argonauts on their quest for the Golden Fleece. The enormous ancient constellation Argo Navis was divided in the 18th century into the keel (Carina), the stern (Puppis), and the sails (Vela).
funFact: Canopus is the second-brightest star in the night sky and contains the Eta Carinae nebula, home to one of the most massive known stars.

name: Cassiopeia
mythology: Cassiopeia was the vain queen of Aethiopia whose boast that she was more beautiful than the sea nymphs brought Poseidon's wrath upon her daughter Andromeda. As punishment she was placed in the sky on her throne, condemned to circle the pole, hanging upside down for half of every night.
funFact: Its unmistakable W shape lies opposite the Big Dipper across the North Star, so one of the two is always high in northern skies.

name: Centaurus
mythology: Centaurus represents Chiron, the wise and gentle centaur who tutored heroes such as Achilles, Jason, and Heracles. Accidentally wounded by one of Heracles' poisoned arrows, the immortal Chiron gave up his immortality to escape the pain and was honored with a place in the sky.
funFact: Alpha Centauri is the closest star system to the Sun at 4.4 light-years, and its faint companion Proxima Centauri is the nearest star of all.

name: Cepheus
mythology: Cepheus was the king of Aethiopia, husband of Cassiopeia and father of Andromeda. When the oracle demanded his daughter be sacrificed to the sea monster Cetus, he reluctantly chained her to the rocks; the whole royal family was later placed in the sky.
funFact: Delta Cephei is the prototype of the Cepheid variable stars, whose pulsations let astronomers measure distances across the universe.

name: Cetus
mythology: Cetus is the sea monster sent by Poseidon to devour Andromeda, turned to stone when Perseus revealed the severed head of Medusa. It swims in the 'Sea' region of the sky among the other watery constellations.
funFact: Contains Mira, 'the Wonderful' — the first variable star ever discovered, which fades and brightens dramatically over an 11-month cycle.

name: Chamaeleon
mythology: Chamaeleon is one of the twelve southern constellations created by the Dutch navigators Keyser and de Houtman in the 1590s, depicting the color-changing lizard they encountered on their voyages to the East Indies.
funFact: On old star maps the chameleon is drawn sticking out its tongue to catch the neighboring constellation Musca, the fly.

name: Circinus
mythology: Circinus is a Lacaille creation from the 1750s, representing the dividers or drawing compass used by draftsmen and navigators. It was placed next to Triangulum Australe, which Lacaille styled as a surveyor's level.
funFact: The fourth-smallest constellation in the sky, squeezed in beside the bright pointer stars of Centaurus.

name: Columba
mythology: Columba, created by Petrus Plancius in 1592, represents the dove Noah released from the Ark to search for dry land. It is also linked to the dove the Argonauts sent ahead to fly between the Clashing Rocks.
funFact: Contains Mu Columbae, a 'runaway star' racing through space after being ejected from the Orion Nebula region millions of years ago.

name: Coma Berenices
mythology: Queen Berenice II of Egypt vowed to sacrifice her beautiful hair to the gods if her husband returned safely from war. When the shorn locks vanished from the temple, the court astronomer declared that the gods had placed them in the sky.
funFact: One of the few constellations named for a real historical person, and home to the North Galactic Pole and a great cluster of galaxies.

name: Corona Australis
mythology: Corona Australis is a wreath or crown lying at the feet of Sagittarius. Some myths call it the crown of laurel that Dionysus placed in the sky in honor of his mother Semele after rescuing her from the underworld.
funFact: Despite its faint stars, its graceful arc was recognized as a constellation by Ptolemy nearly 2,000 years ago.

name: Corona Borealis
mythology: Corona Borealis is the jeweled crown of Ariadne, the Cretan princess who helped Theseus escape the labyrinth of the Minotaur. When the god Dionysus married her, he tossed her wedding crown into the sky, where its gems became stars.
funFact: Contains T Coronae Borealis, the 'Blaze Star', a recurrent nova that dramatically brightens to naked-eye visibility roughly every 80 years.

name: Corvus
mythology: Apollo sent the crow with a cup (Crater) to fetch water, but the bird dallied waiting for figs to ripen and returned late, blaming a water snake (Hydra). Seeing through the lie, Apollo cast crow, cup, and snake into the sky, where the crow is forever kept from drinking.
funFact: Its four brightest stars form a distinctive quadrilateral called 'the Sail', which points the way to bright Spica in Virgo.

name: Crater
mythology: Crater is the cup of Apollo, carried by the crow Corvus in the myth of the bird's failed errand for water. It sits on the coils of Hydra beside the crow, forever just out of the thirsty bird's reach.
funFact: Its name is the origin of the word 'crater' — the Greek krater was a wide bowl used for mixing wine and water.

name: Crux
mythology: Crux, the Southern Cross, was visible to the ancient Greeks who counted its stars as part of Centaurus, but precession carried it below their horizon. European navigators of the 16th century adopted it as a guide, since its long axis points toward the south celestial pole.
funFact: The smallest of all 88 constellations, yet featured on the flags of Australia, New Zealand, Brazil, and several other nations.

name: Cygnus
mythology: Cygnus is a swan flying south along the Milky Way, often identified with Zeus, who took a swan's form to seduce Leda, queen of Sparta. Another tale makes it Cycnus, the devoted friend of Phaethon, who dove repeatedly into the river Eridanus to retrieve his friend's body and was transformed into a swan.
funFact: Also called the Northern Cross; Albireo at the swan's head is a beloved double star of contrasting gold and sapphire, and Cygnus X-1 was the first widely accepted black hole.

name: Delphinus
mythology: Delphinus is the dolphin that persuaded the sea nymph Amphitrite to marry Poseidon, or in another tale the dolphin that rescued the musician Arion, who leapt overboard to escape murderous sailors and was carried safely to shore on its back.
funFact: Its stars Sualocin and Rotanev spell 'Nicolaus Venator' backwards — a Latin form of Niccolò Cacciatore, an assistant astronomer who slyly named them after himself.

name: Dorado
mythology: Dorado was introduced by Keyser and de Houtman in the 1590s, representing the mahi-mahi or dolphinfish the Dutch sailors watched chasing flying fish (the neighboring constellation Volans) in tropical seas.
funFact: Contains most of the Large Magellanic Cloud, the biggest satellite galaxy of the Milky Way, and the spectacular Tarantula Nebula.

name: Draco
mythology: Draco is Ladon, the hundred-headed dragon that guarded the golden apples in the garden of the Hesperides, slain by Heracles as one of his twelve labors. The dragon coils between the two bears around the north celestial pole.
funFact: Thuban was the pole star when the Egyptian pyramids were built around 2700 BC; Earth's axial precession has since shifted the pole to Polaris.

name: Equuleus
mythology: Equuleus, the little horse or foal, is sometimes identified as Celeris, the swift brother or offspring of the winged horse Pegasus, given to the hero Castor by the god Hermes.
funFact: The second-smallest constellation in the sky; only the head of the foal is depicted, peeking out beside Pegasus.

name: Eridanus
mythology: Eridanus is the river into which Phaethon fell after losing control of the sun chariot of his father Helios, scorching the earth until Zeus struck him down with a thunderbolt. It has been identified with the Po, the Nile, and other great rivers.
funFact: The sixth-largest constellation, winding from Orion's foot deep into the southern sky, ending at brilliant Achernar — 'the river's end'.

name: Fornax
mythology: Fornax is a Lacaille constellation from the 1750s, originally 'Fornax Chemica', the chemical furnace, honoring the apparatus of laboratory chemistry and, by tradition, the great chemist Antoine Lavoisier.
funFact: Home to the Fornax Cluster of galaxies and the Hubble Ultra Deep Field, one of the deepest views of the universe ever taken.

name: Gemini
mythology: Gemini represents the twins Castor and Pollux, born to Leda but with different fathers: Castor mortal, Pollux immortal as a son of Zeus. When Castor was killed, Pollux begged to share his immortality with his brother, so Zeus placed them together in the sky.
funFact: Castor, seemingly a single star, is actually a sextuple system of six suns bound together; the Geminid meteor shower radiates from here every December.

name: Grus
mythology: Grus, the long-necked crane, was introduced by Keyser and de Houtman in the 1590s. In ancient Egypt the crane was a symbol of the astronomer, making it a fitting addition to the sky; its stars were once part of Piscis Austrinus.
funFact: Its two brightest stars, Alnair and Tiaki, make it one of the easier far-southern constellations to recognize.

name: Hercules
mythology: Hercules is the Roman name of Heracles, the greatest of Greek heroes, famed for his twelve labors. Curiously, the sky shows him upside down, kneeling with one foot on the head of Draco, the dragon he slew in the garden of the Hesperides.
funFact: Contains the Great Globular Cluster M13, a ball of several hundred thousand stars, and the 'Keystone' asterism that marks the hero's torso.

name: Horologium
mythology: Horologium is a Lacaille constellation honoring the pendulum clock invented by Christiaan Huygens in 1656, an instrument essential to the precise astronomical observations of the age.
funFact: On old charts, the constellation's faint stars trace the clock's pendulum and weights, with the brightest star marking the clock face.

name: Hydra
mythology: Hydra is the many-headed serpent of Lerna slain by Heracles as his second labor: each severed head grew back two more until his nephew Iolaus cauterized the stumps with fire. In the sky it also plays the water snake blamed by the lying crow Corvus.
funFact: The largest of all 88 constellations, stretching more than a quarter of the way around the sky; its lone bright star Alphard means 'the solitary one'.

name: Hydrus
mythology: Hydrus is a small southern water snake introduced by Keyser and de Houtman, likely inspired by the sea snakes Dutch sailors saw on their voyages to the East Indies. It winds between the two Magellanic Clouds.
funFact: Beta Hydri is the closest reasonably bright star to the south celestial pole, and is one of the oldest sun-like stars in our neighborhood.

name: Indus
mythology: Indus, created by Keyser and de Houtman, depicts an indigenous man holding arrows or spears, representing the native peoples encountered by Dutch explorers on their voyages to the East Indies and beyond.
funFact: Epsilon Indi, just 12 light-years away, is one of the nearest sun-like stars and a prime target in the search for habitable planets.

name: Lacerta
mythology: Lacerta was formed by Johannes Hevelius in 1687 from faint stars between Cygnus and Andromeda. He chose a lizard, he said, because nothing larger would fit in the narrow gap.
funFact: Its zigzag of faint stars earns it the nickname 'Little Cassiopeia'; the mysterious object BL Lacertae here turned out to be the beacon of a distant galaxy's black hole.

name: Leo
mythology: Leo is the Nemean Lion, a beast with an impenetrable hide that Heracles strangled with his bare hands as the first of his twelve labors. He wore its pelt ever after as armor. The lion's head is traced by the famous 'Sickle' of stars.
funFact: Regulus, 'the little king', sits almost exactly on the ecliptic and is regularly occulted by the Moon; the Leonid meteor storm radiates from the Sickle each November.

name: Leo Minor
mythology: Leo Minor is a lion cub placed by Hevelius in 1687 in the blank space between the great lion Leo and the Great Bear. It has no classical mythology of its own.
funFact: Due to a cataloguing oversight, Leo Minor has a Beta star but no star labeled Alpha.

name: Lepus
mythology: Lepus is a hare crouching at the feet of Orion, perpetually pursued across the sky by the hunter and his dogs. Some say Hermes placed the hare in the sky for its swiftness.
funFact: Home to Hind's Crimson Star, a variable star so deeply red that observers have compared it to a drop of blood on black velvet.

name: Libra
mythology: Libra, the scales of justice, is the only zodiac constellation representing an object rather than a creature. To the Greeks its stars were the claws of the neighboring Scorpion, a history preserved in its star names Zubenelgenubi and Zubeneschamali — the southern and northern claws.
funFact: Zubeneschamali is often reported by observers as the only naked-eye star with a greenish tint — though photographs show it as white.

name: Lupus
mythology: Lupus is a wild beast impaled on a pole by the neighboring Centaurus, being carried as an offering to the altar Ara. Greek and Roman astronomers called it simply 'the Beast'; the wolf identity came later through translations.
funFact: In 1006 AD a supernova in Lupus became the brightest stellar event in recorded history, visible in daylight and casting shadows at night.

name: Lynx
mythology: Lynx was created by Hevelius in 1687 to fill the faint gap between Ursa Major and Auriga. He named it the lynx, joking that only the lynx-eyed — those with exceptional sight — would be able to see it.
funFact: True to its name, this large constellation contains almost nothing visible to the casual eye; finding it is a genuine test of dark skies.

name: Lyra
mythology: Lyra is the lyre of Orpheus, whose music charmed wild beasts, rivers, and even Hades himself when Orpheus descended to the underworld to plead for his wife Eurydice. After his death the Muses placed his lyre among the stars.
funFact: Vega was the first star ever photographed, will be our pole star in about 12,000 years, and anchors the Summer Triangle; nearby lies the famous Ring Nebula.

name: Mensa
mythology: Mensa is the only constellation named after a real geographic feature: Table Mountain at the Cape of Good Hope, where Lacaille made his southern star catalog in the 1750s. The Large Magellanic Cloud hovers above it like the famous 'tablecloth' of cloud over the real mountain.
funFact: The faintest constellation in the entire sky — its brightest star is barely magnitude 5.

name: Microscopium
mythology: Microscopium is a Lacaille constellation honoring the compound microscope, another of the scientific instruments he enshrined in the southern sky in the 1750s.
funFact: About 3,800 years ago, Gamma Microscopii passed within a few light-years of the Sun and would have outshone Sirius in our sky.

name: Monoceros
mythology: Monoceros, the unicorn, was introduced by Petrus Plancius in 1613 in the dim region inside the Winter Triangle. The unicorn was a popular symbol of purity in medieval Europe, though the constellation has no classical myth.
funFact: Though faint, it is rich in deep-sky treasures: the Rosette Nebula, the Christmas Tree Cluster, and Plaskett's Star, one of the most massive binaries known.

name: Musca
mythology: Musca, the fly, is a Keyser and de Houtman creation just south of the Southern Cross. It was originally called Apis, the bee, until Lacaille renamed it to avoid confusion — leaving the neighboring Chamaeleon forever poised to eat it.
funFact: The only officially recognized insect in the sky (the bee was demoted).

name: Norma
mythology: Norma is a Lacaille constellation representing a carpenter's set square, placed beside the level (his original name for Triangulum Australe) and the compasses (Circinus) as a trio of craftsman's tools.
funFact: The Milky Way runs richly through Norma, and the 'Great Attractor' — a mysterious mass pulling our galaxy through space — lies in this direction.

name: Octans
mythology: Octans, another Lacaille invention, honors the octant, the navigational instrument invented by John Hadley in 1730 that evolved into the sextant. Fittingly, it contains the south celestial pole itself.
funFact: The southern 'pole star', Sigma Octantis, is so faint that navigators use the Southern Cross to find south instead.

name: Ophiuchus
mythology: Ophiuchus is Asclepius, the great healer taught by the centaur Chiron, shown grasping a huge serpent — the source of his medical wisdom. When he grew so skilled that he could raise the dead, Hades complained, and Zeus struck him down but honored him with a place in the sky.
funFact: The Sun spends more time crossing Ophiuchus each December than it does crossing neighboring Scorpius — making it the unofficial '13th zodiac constellation'.

name: Orion
mythology: Orion was a giant huntsman who boasted he could slay every animal on Earth, so Gaia sent a scorpion to kill him. Zeus placed both in the sky at opposite ends: as Scorpius rises in the east, Orion flees below the western horizon, and the two are never seen together.
funFact: The most recognizable constellation in the sky, visible from every inhabited place on Earth; below the three Belt stars hangs the Orion Nebula, a stellar nursery visible to the naked eye.

name: Pavo
mythology: Pavo, the peacock, was introduced by Keyser and de Houtman. In Greek myth the peacock was sacred to Hera, who set the hundred eyes of her slain watchman Argus into its tail — a story the Dutch navigators may have had in mind.
funFact: Its brightest star is officially named 'Peacock' — the name was assigned in the 1930s because Royal Air Force navigation manuals required every bright star to have a proper name.

name: Pegasus
mythology: Pegasus is the winged horse that sprang from the neck of Medusa when Perseus beheaded her. Tamed by the hero Bellerophon, Pegasus helped slay the Chimera, but threw his rider when Bellerophon arrogantly tried to fly to Olympus; the horse completed the journey alone.
funFact: The Great Square of Pegasus is a signpost of the autumn sky; 51 Pegasi hosts the first planet ever discovered orbiting another sun-like star.

name: Perseus
mythology: Perseus beheaded the gorgon Medusa, whose gaze turned men to stone, then rescued the princess Andromeda from the sea monster Cetus on his way home. In the sky he holds Medusa's severed head, marked by the 'demon star' Algol.
funFact: Algol dims sharply every 2.9 days as one star of the pair eclipses the other — its startling 'winking' earned it the name 'head of the demon'; the Perseid meteors radiate from here each August.

name: Phoenix
mythology: Phoenix, introduced by Keyser and de Houtman, depicts the mythical firebird that lives for centuries, then burns itself on a pyre and rises reborn from its own ashes — an ancient symbol of renewal in Egyptian, Greek, and Chinese traditions.
funFact: The largest of the twelve constellations created from the Dutch navigators' southern observations.

name: Pictor
mythology: Pictor is a Lacaille constellation, originally 'Equuleus Pictoris', the painter's easel, continuing his theme of celebrating the arts and sciences in the southern sky.
funFact: Beta Pictoris is surrounded by a spectacular disk of gas and dust where planets are forming — one of the first such disks ever imaged.

name: Pisces
mythology: Pisces represents Aphrodite and her son Eros, who leapt into the Euphrates and became fishes (or were rescued by them) to escape the monster Typhon. The two fish are tied together by a cord so they would not lose each other.
funFact: Contains the vernal equinox point, where the Sun crosses the celestial equator each March — the zero point of the celestial coordinate system.

name: Piscis Austrinus
mythology: Piscis Austrinus is the great southern fish, said to be the parent of the zodiac fishes Pisces. It drinks the stream of water poured from the jar of Aquarius, and in Syrian myth it rescued the goddess Derceto from a lake.
funFact: Fomalhaut, 'the fish's mouth', is called 'the loneliest star' — the only bright star in a wide stretch of autumn sky — and hosts a famous debris ring imaged by Hubble.

name: Puppis
mythology: Puppis is the stern or poop deck of the Argo, the ship of Jason and the Argonauts, formed when the huge ancient constellation Argo Navis was split into three parts by Lacaille in the 18th century.
funFact: Naos is one of the hottest naked-eye stars known, blazing at over 40,000 degrees — seven times hotter than the Sun.

name: Pyxis
mythology: Pyxis, the mariner's magnetic compass, was added by Lacaille near the mast of the old ship Argo. Though it sails with the ship's remnants, it was not part of the ancient vessel — magnetic compasses were unknown to the Greeks.
funFact: T Pyxidis here is a recurrent nova that has erupted at least six times since 1890.

name: Reticulum
mythology: Reticulum honors the reticle — the grid of fine crosshairs in Lacaille's telescope eyepiece that he used to measure the positions of nearly 10,000 southern stars from the Cape of Good Hope.
funFact: A tiny diamond of stars near the Large Magellanic Cloud; Zeta Reticuli is a close pair of sun-like stars visible as a naked-eye double under dark skies.

name: Sagitta
mythology: Sagitta is an arrow — perhaps the one Heracles used to slay the eagle that tormented Prometheus, or a shaft belonging to Eros. It flies between the Swan and the Eagle, high in the summer Milky Way.
funFact: The third-smallest constellation, yet its arrow shape is surprisingly easy to spot inside the Summer Triangle.

name: Sagittarius
mythology: Sagittarius is a centaur archer, often identified with Crotus, the inventor of archery who lived among the Muses. His arrow points at the heart of the Scorpion, ready to avenge Orion should the scorpion ever attack again.
funFact: Its central stars form the famous 'Teapot', and the steam from its spout marks the direction of the Milky Way's center and its supermassive black hole.

name: Scorpius
mythology: Scorpius is the scorpion sent by Gaia to sting the boastful hunter Orion. The two enemies were placed at opposite ends of the sky, so that Orion sets as the Scorpion rises and they never meet.
funFact: Antares, 'the rival of Mars', is a red supergiant so vast that placed at the Sun's position it would swallow the orbit of Mars.

name: Sculptor
mythology: Sculptor is a Lacaille constellation, originally 'l'Atelier du Sculpteur' — the sculptor's studio, complete with a carved head on a tripod table and the artist's mallet and chisels.
funFact: Contains the South Galactic Pole and the beautiful Sculptor Galaxy (NGC 253), one of the brightest spiral galaxies beyond our Local Group.

name: Scutum
mythology: Scutum, created by Hevelius in 1684, honors King John III Sobieski of Poland, who had defeated the Ottoman army at the Battle of Vienna the year before — and who funded the rebuilding of Hevelius's observatory after a fire. It is the only constellation born of a political tribute still in use.
funFact: The Scutum Star Cloud is one of the brightest patches of the Milky Way, called by Barnard 'the gem of the Milky Way'.

name: Serpens
mythology: Serpens is the great snake held by Ophiuchus, the healer Asclepius. Snakes, which shed their skin and appear reborn, were symbols of renewal and healing — the origin of the serpent-entwined staff still used as a medical emblem today.
funFact: The only constellation split into two separate pieces: Serpens Caput (the head) and Serpens Cauda (the tail), divided by the serpent bearer.

name: Sextans
mythology: Sextans was created by Hevelius in 1687 to commemorate the large sextant he used to measure star positions — an instrument destroyed when fire consumed his observatory in 1679. Famously, he preferred measuring with the naked eye over the telescope.
funFact: A dim constellation riding the celestial equator between Leo and Hydra.

name: Taurus
mythology: Taurus is the bull whose form Zeus assumed to carry off the princess Europa across the sea to Crete. Only the front half of the bull is shown, charging at Orion with the red eye of Aldebaran and horns tipped by bright stars.
funFact: Contains two of the finest naked-eye star clusters — the Pleiades (Seven Sisters) and the V-shaped Hyades — plus the Crab Nebula, remnant of a supernova seen in 1054 AD.

name: Telescopium
mythology: Telescopium is a Lacaille constellation honoring the aerial telescope — the giant long-focus refractors of the 17th century. It completes his celestial museum of scientific instruments.
funFact: In 2020 astronomers reported a black hole in a naked-eye star system here (HR 6819), though later work suggests it is a rare pair of exotic stars instead.

name: Triangulum Australe
mythology: Triangulum Australe, the southern triangle, first appeared on globes around 1600 based on the observations of Keyser and de Houtman. Lacaille later drew it as a surveyor's level, grouping it with his other craftsman's tools nearby.
funFact: Its three brightest stars form a nearly perfect equilateral triangle — more convincing than its faint northern namesake.

name: Triangulum
mythology: Triangulum is one of Ptolemy's original 48 constellations. The Greeks called it Deltoton for its resemblance to the capital letter delta, and associated it with the Nile delta or the island of Sicily.
funFact: Home to the Triangulum Galaxy (M33), the third-largest member of our Local Group and, for sharp-eyed observers under pristine skies, the most distant naked-eye object.

name: Tucana
mythology: Tucana, the toucan, was introduced by Keyser and de Houtman, celebrating the huge-billed bird of the South American tropics — a token of the exotic lands opened by the age of exploration.
funFact: Contains the Small Magellanic Cloud and 47 Tucanae, the second-brightest globular cluster in the sky with over a million stars.

name: Ursa Major
mythology: Ursa Major is Callisto, a nymph loved by Zeus and transformed into a bear by the jealous Hera. Years later her son Arcas nearly killed her while hunting, so Zeus placed them both in the sky. Hera, still angry, persuaded the sea gods never to let the bears bathe — which is why they never set below northern horizons.
funFact: Its seven brightest stars form the Big Dipper, the most famous star pattern on Earth; Mizar and Alcor in the handle are the classic naked-eye 'eyesight test' double.

name: Ursa Minor
mythology: Ursa Minor is Arcas, son of Callisto, placed in the sky beside his mother — or in older tales one of the nymphs who nursed the infant Zeus on Crete. Its tail star is Polaris, the pivot around which the whole northern sky appears to turn.
funFact: Polaris, the North Star, sits within a degree of the celestial pole and has guided travelers for centuries — but it is only the 48th-brightest star in the sky.

name: Vela
mythology: Vela represents the sails of the Argo, the ship that carried Jason and the Argonauts, created when the vast ancient constellation Argo Navis was divided by Lacaille into keel, stern, and sails.
funFact: Contains the Vela Pulsar, the spinning corpse of a star that exploded about 11,000 years ago, flashing eleven times a second.

name: Virgo
mythology: Virgo is usually identified with Dike or Astraea, goddess of justice, who lived among humans during the Golden Age but fled to the heavens as humanity grew wicked. She is also seen as Demeter, the harvest goddess, holding an ear of wheat marked by the bright star Spica.
funFact: The second-largest constellation and home to the Virgo Cluster of some 2,000 galaxies, the heart of our local supercluster; the first-ever image of a black hole was taken in M87 here.

name: Volans
mythology: Volans, the flying fish, was introduced by Keyser and de Houtman after the tropical fish that glide over the waves on wing-like fins — often depicted being chased by the dolphinfish Dorado, just as sailors saw at sea.
funFact: On old star charts the flying fish is shown leaping over the ship Argo Navis.

name: Vulpecula
mythology: Vulpecula was created by Hevelius in 1687 as 'Vulpecula cum Ansere' — the little fox with the goose in its jaws. The goose has since been dropped from the name but survives in the title of the constellation's brightest star, Anser.
funFact: The first pulsar ever discovered — the 'LGM-1' signal briefly suspected to be aliens — was found here in 1967, along with the famous Dumbbell Nebula.
